name: Kiselev Black Hole
description: Schwarzschild's black hole with one more term in its metric, a power of the radius that stands for matter around the hole whose pressure, averaged over directions, is a fixed multiple of its energy density. Valery Kiselev wrote it down in 2003 as a black hole surrounded by quintessence, and Matt Visser showed in 2020 that the matter is neither a perfect fluid nor quintessence.
convention: The Schwarzschild radius is $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, and $r_q$ is a length. We keep factors of $c$ explicit.
history: Every black hole sits in a universe whose expansion is speeding up: two teams measuring distant supernovae of type Ia, one with Adam Riess and one with Saul Perlmutter as first author, found that in 1998 and 1999 [riess1998, perlmutter1999]. A cosmological constant does that, and so does any matter whose pressure $p = w\rho$ is negative enough, $w < -1/3$ [kiselev2003]. Robert Caldwell, Rahul Dave, and Paul Steinhardt gave such a component the name "quintessence" in 1998 and modelled it as a scalar field evolving in a potential [caldwell1998]. For the cosmological constant the black hole was already known: Friedrich Kottler had found it in 1918 [kottler1918]. What does a black hole look like with quintessence around it?¶A fluid has one pressure, the same in whichever direction you push on it [visser2020]. For static, spherically symmetric matter with one pressure the equations had given, in Valery Kiselev's words, a metric with "no horizon, no 'hair' and no black hole" [kiselev2003]. So in 2003 he let the pressure along the radius differ from the pressure around the sphere, asked that their average over directions be $w\rho$, and fixed their ratio by one demand, $T_t{}^t = T_r{}^r$ [kiselev2003]. He called it a "principle of additivity and linearity": with it $g_{tt}g_{rr} = -1$, Einstein's equations become linear in the one function $f = -g_{tt}$, and solutions add like ingredients in a pot, each kind of matter putting its own power of $r$ into $f$ [kiselev2003]. Matter of state parameter $w$ puts in $-(r_q/r)^{3w+1}$, with $r_q$ a length that sets how much of it there is [kiselev2003]: $$f(r) = 1 - \frac{r_s}{r} - \left(\frac{r_q}{r}\right)^{3w+1}.$$¶The black holes already known are special cases [kiselev2003]. Dust, $w = 0$, puts in a term in $1/r$, which is one more mass [kiselev2003]. Radiation's $w = 1/3$, with the sign of the term reversed, gives the $1/r^2$ of Reissner and Nordström's electric charge [kiselev2003]. The cosmological constant is $w = -1$ and gives Kottler's $r^2$ [kiselev2003]. All of them have a radial pressure equal to minus the energy density, and Ted Jacobson proved in 2007 that $g_{tt}g_{rr} = -1$ holds exactly then, with $r$ an affine parameter along every radial light ray [jacobson2007].¶Kiselev worked one new case through, $w = -2/3$, where the added term is linear in $r$ and $f = 1 - r_s/r - r/r_q$ [kiselev2003]. For $r_q > 4r_s$ this black hole has two horizons, an inner one around the hole and an outer one far from it, with a static region between them [kiselev2003]. Take the hole away and the matter alone still has a horizon, at $r = r_q$, "of de Sitter kind" [kiselev2003]. Each horizon has a Gibbons-Hawking temperature, and the matter cools the black hole, whose horizon is colder than Schwarzschild's for the same $r_s$ [kiselev2003, gibbons1977]. The matter at this $w$ satisfies the dominant energy condition, which Mirjam Cvetič, Gary Gibbons, and Christopher Pope found to hold whenever $|3w + 1| \le 2$ and the energy density is positive [cvetic2016].¶By 2019 the metric had, by Matt Visser's count, "over 200 direct and indirect citations" [visser2020]. Songbai Chen and Jiliang Jing rang it like a bell and found that with the matter there a scalar wave "damps more rapidly" [chen2005]. Sushant Ghosh set it spinning with Newman and Janis's algorithm, and Bobir Toshmatov, Zdeněk Stuchlík, and Bobomurat Ahmedov did the same with a variant of it [ghosh2016, toshmatov2017, newman1965janis]. Most of those papers, Visser found, called the matter a perfect fluid and called it quintessence [visser2020].¶Is the matter either of those? A fluid's pressure is the same in every direction, and here the pressure along the radius is $-\rho$ while the pressure around the sphere is $(3w + 1)\rho/2$, equal only at $w = -1$ [visser2020]. Kiselev's own calculation averages the pressures over directions to get $w$, and his closing discussion then calls the matter "a perfect fluid" [kiselev2003, visser2020]. Visser's quickest test needs no calculation: at $w = 1/3$ the matter is the electric field of a charge, which is no fluid and no quintessence [visser2020]. Quintessence, as cosmologists use the word, is a scalar field that changes in time, and its stress tensor is a perfect fluid's [visser2020]. With Petarpa Boonserm, Tritos Ngampitipan, and Alex Simpson he then split Kiselev's stress tensor into a perfect fluid carrying an electric or a scalar charge and the field of that charge, which measures how far the matter is from a fluid [boonserm2020].

related.text: Kiselev's black hole at $w = 0$, where the added term is $r_q/r$ and the metric is Schwarzschild's with radius $r_s + r_q$. Dust at rest adds mass and nothing else [kiselev2003].
Kiselev's black hole at $w = -1$, where the added term is $r^2/r_q^2$: Kottler's metric with $\Lambda = 3/r_q^2$, the matter a cosmological constant [kiselev2003].

At $w = 1/3$ the added term goes as $1/r^2$, and with its sign reversed the metric is Reissner-Nordström's. Visser pointed to this case: the matter is then an electric field, which is no perfect fluid [kiselev2003, visser2020].

At $w = -1/3$ the added term, which Visser writes $K/r^{3w+1}$, is a constant, and $f = 1 - K - r_s/r$ is the metric outside a global monopole with solid angle deficit $K$. Kiselev noted the "angle defect" of the spheres himself [kiselev2003, visser2020, barriola1989].

Kiselev's metric at $w = -1$ with no black hole, $r_s = 0$ and $\Lambda = 3/r_q^2$. Kiselev set his matter at $w = -2/3$ beside it: near the horizon the two metrics agree up to a constant conformal factor [kiselev2003].
Kiselev's matter alone at $w = -2/3$ is conformal to the part $\tau + \rho > 0$ of Minkowski space, with the factor $4r_q^2/(\tau + \rho)^2$ [kiselev2003].

coordinates.name: Static Spherical

parameters.description: Normalisation length of the surrounding matter
State parameter, the ratio of the pressure averaged over directions to the energy density
Kiselev's term in the metric function

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, and take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$. We write Kiselev's term as $h = (r_q/r)^{3w + 1}$.
geodesics: \ddot{r} - \dfrac{\left(r\,h - r + r_s\right)\left(r\,h\left(3w + 1\right) + r_s\right)}{2r^3}\dot{t}^2 - \dfrac{r\,h\left(3w + 1\right) + r_s}{2r\left(r - r_s - r\,h\right)}\dot{r}^2 + \left(r\,h - r + r_s\right)\dot{\theta}^2 + \left(r\,h - r + r_s\right)\sin^2\theta\,\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

coordinates.name: Ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Normalisation length of the surrounding matter
State parameter, the ratio of the pressure averaged over directions to the energy density
Kiselev's term in the metric function

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the advanced time $v = ct + r_*$ a length, where $dr_*/dr = \left(1 - r_s/r - h\right)^{-1}$, $r_* = 0$ at $r = 0$, and $h = (r_q/r)^{3w + 1}$ is Kiselev's term.
geodesics: \ddot{r} - \dfrac{\left(r\,h - r + r_s\right)\left(r\,h\left(3w + 1\right) + r_s\right)}{2r^3}\dot{v}^2 - \dfrac{r\,h\left(3w + 1\right) + r_s}{r^2}\dot{v}\dot{r} + \left(r\,h - r + r_s\right)\dot{\theta}^2 + \left(r\,h - r + r_s\right)\sin^2\theta\,\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

coordinates.name: Outgoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Normalisation length of the surrounding matter
State parameter, the ratio of the pressure averaged over directions to the energy density
Kiselev's term in the metric function

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(u, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the retarded time $u = ct - r_*$ a length, where $dr_*/dr = \left(1 - r_s/r - h\right)^{-1}$, $r_* = 0$ at $r = 0$, and $h = (r_q/r)^{3w + 1}$ is Kiselev's term.
geodesics: \ddot{r} - \dfrac{\left(r\,h - r + r_s\right)\left(r\,h\left(3w + 1\right) + r_s\right)}{2r^3}\dot{u}^2 + \dfrac{r\,h\left(3w + 1\right) + r_s}{r^2}\dot{u}\dot{r} + \left(r\,h - r + r_s\right)\dot{\theta}^2 + \left(r\,h - r + r_s\right)\sin^2\theta\,\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

coordinates.name: Static, Linear Term

parameters.description: Normalisation length of the surrounding matter

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, and take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$. The state parameter is $w = -2/3$, and for $r_q > 4r_s$ the horizons are $r_\pm = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(r_q \pm \sqrt{r_q^2 - 4r_qr_s}\right)$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
geodesics: \ddot{r} + \dfrac{\left(r^2 - r_s\,r_q\right)\left(r^2 - r\,r_q + r_s\,r_q\right)}{2r^3\,r_q^2}\dot{t}^2 - \dfrac{r^2 - r_s\,r_q}{2r\left(r^2 - r\,r_q + r_s\,r_q\right)}\dot{r}^2 + \dfrac{r^2 - r\,r_q + r_s\,r_q}{r_q}\dot{\theta}^2 + \dfrac{\left(r^2 - r\,r_q + r_s\,r_q\right)\sin^2\theta}{r_q}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

coordinates.name: Free Matter, Hyperbolic

parameters.description: Normalisation length of the surrounding matter

coordinates.convention: We use dimensionless coordinates $(\eta, \chi, \theta, \phi)$, with $\eta = ct/2r_q$ and $\chi = -\tfrac{1}{2}\ln(1 - r/r_q)$ in the static coordinates at $w = -2/3$ and $r_s = 0$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Free Matter, Conformally Flat

parameters.description: Normalisation length of the surrounding matter

coordinates.convention: We use dimensionless coordinates $(\tau, \rho, \theta, \phi)$, with $\tau = e^{\eta}\cosh\chi$ and $\rho = e^{\eta}\sinh\chi$ in the hyperbolic coordinates $\eta$ and $\chi$, so the areal radius is $r = 2r_q\rho/(\tau + \rho)$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
